record.description: Christ's recapitulation as solution to human incapacity. Structure: (1) Problem: After the fall, humans "fell under the power of sin" (AH III.18.2; Book III is preserved in Latin translation). (2) Human INCAPACITY: "Those who could not save themselves" (AH III.20.3; text extant only in the Latin version, SC 211 Rousseau–Doutreleau — no Greek is transmitted for this sentence). (3) Paul proves "the weakness of man" via Rom 7:18, 24. (4) solution: Christ "recapitulates" human history, accomplishing what humans cannot. (5) Salvation is "not by ourselves but by God's assistance." tension: Irenaeus affirms both free will (AH IV.37) AND human incapacity (AH III.20). Resolution: Free will for moral choices; incapacity for salvific self-rescue. More Pauline than other Apologists.
record.label: Irenaeus' Recapitulation Theodicy (AH III.18-20)

metadata.author: Irenaeus

conclusion.text: Christ's recapitulation is the necessary divine solution to post-lapsarian human incapacity for self-salvation, such that human free will operates within moral deliberation but cannot achieve salvation without divine assistance.

premises.text: After the fall, humans fell under the power of sin (Latin version only, SC 211).
Those who fell under sin's power could not save themselves (AH III.20.3; text extant only in the Latin version, SC 211 Rousseau–Doutreleau — no Greek is transmitted for this sentence).

Paul's testimony in Romans 7:18, 24 demonstrates the weakness of man (τὴν ἀσθένειαν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου), specifically that 'good does not dwell in my flesh' and that the wretched human requires deliverance from outside.
Christ 'recapitulates' (ἀνακεφαλαιόω) human history by uniting the divine and human in himself, thereby accomplishing what humans cannot accomplish for themselves.
Salvation is achieved not by human effort but by God's assistance.
Irenaeus affirms free will (autexousion) in moral contexts (AH IV.37), but this free will does not extend to salvific self-rescue from post-lapsarian incapacity.

validity_assessment.rationale: The argument is formally valid if P4 (recapitulation as divine action) is granted as bridging the gap between P2 (incapacity) and the conclusion. However, scholarly acceptance of this validity is disputed because: (1) the tension between P6 (free will affirmation) and P2 (incapacity) requires the ad hoc distinction between moral and salvific capacities that is not fully explicit in Irenaeus' text; (2) the precise scope of autexousion in Irenaeus remains contested (see theological loading note); (3) the argument's validity depends on accepting a Pauline (Romans 7) anthropology that some scholars argue Irenaeus imports rather than develops organically. The argument is dialectically persuasive within Irenaeus' framework but not formally valid without the reconstructed P6, which itself requires modern scholarly supplementation.
validity_assessment.scholarly_consensus: The structure is widely accepted as Irenaean, but the precise resolution of the free-will/incapacity tension remains debated. Osborn (2001) and Behr (2013) differ on whether Irenaeus achieves a coherent synthesis or leaves an aporetic tension.

premises.text: God created human beings with autexousion (self-determining power) from the beginning, such that humans possess their own power to achieve the good of their own free will.
This freedom is structurally constitutive of human nature, not incidental to it.
The goodness of virtue requires that virtue be chosen rather than compelled; if humans were created perfect by necessity, they would not truly possess virtue.
God does not coerce or compel human beings, for coercion would reduce humans to puppets rather than rational agents.
The Gnostic view that spiritual natures (pneumatikoi) are saved by necessity and material natures (hylikoi) are damned by necessity denies genuine personhood and moral agency.
Humans were created 'unfinished' or immature (nepios), requiring moral development toward perfection through experience.
Moral growth requires freedom to choose good over evil through experience.
Christ assumed full human nature including free will in order to redeem it.

metadata.provenance_note: ambiguous: 5 works by Irenaeus of Lyon
metadata.targets: Attacks Valentinian Gnosticism, Marcionite dualism, astrological fatalism, and any system that denies universal human nature and capacity for freedom

validity_assessment.rationale: The argument proceeds through multiple inferential steps that are dialectical rather than formally deductive. P1-P3 establish a definition of human nature; P4-P5 introduce a reductio of the Gnostic position; P6-P7 add a developmental teleology; P8 introduces a Christological premise. The conclusion requires synthesis across theological anthropology, moral psychology, soteriology, and anti-heretical polemic. The inference from 'virtue requires free choice' to 'determinism destroys genuine humanity' involves suppressed premises about the nature of personhood that Irenaeus assumes but does not formally demonstrate. The argument is better understood as a cumulative case or rhetorical synkrisis than as a formally valid syllogism. Scholarly acceptance of the argument's soundness varies: the coherence of Irenaeus's position is generally accepted (e.g., Osborn 2001; Behr 2013), but whether it successfully refutes Gnostic determinism is disputed, since Gnostics might accept that 'genuine humanity' is not their concern—salvation of the spiritual element is.
validity_assessment.scholarly_consensus: The attribution of autexousion-theology to Irenaeus is well-established; the formal validity of his anti-Gnostic argument is rarely assessed in strictly logical terms, with most scholars treating it as a rhetorical-theological construction (see Briggman 2012; Minns 2010).

record.description: Bishop of Lyon (c. 130 — d. 202 CE), originally from Asia Minor, where he heard Polycarp of Smyrna, a direct link to the apostolic generation. His five-book Adversus Haereses, written against Valentinian and other Gnostic systems, contains one of the earliest sustained Christian theologies of human freedom. In AH IV.37, Irenaeus deploys the key Greek term autexousion (rendered in the Latin translation as "liber in arbitrio," free in judgment) to assert that human self-determination and God's counseling nature (to symbouleutikon tou theou) are complementary: God advises but does not compel, so that obedience has genuine moral worth. This argument targets directly the Gnostic tripartition of humanity into predetermined spiritual classes (pneumatikoi, psychikoi, hylikoi), which Irenaeus views as destroying both moral responsibility and the coherence of divine commandments. His anti-Gnostic case extends the earlier reasoning of Justin Martyr (1 Apol. 43-44) and the "futility of sanctions" argument: if human choices are predetermined, praise, blame, law, and punishment become meaningless. Alongside this robust defense of freedom, Irenaeus develops a distinctive recapitulation theodicy (AH III.18-20) acknowledging post-lapsarian human incapacity — "those who could not save themselves" (tous me dynamenous sozein heautous) — resolved by Christ's recapitulation (anakephalaiosis) of human history. He also articulates the nepios doctrine: Adam and Eve were created as moral infants (nepioi), not yet capable of perfection, so that the Fall reflects immature freedom rather than radical depravity. This developmental anthropology, moving from "good" (agathos) to "perfect" (teleios), distinguishes Irenaeus from later Augustinian accounts and parallels the contemporary infant-Adam formulations of Theophilus of Antioch (Ad Autolycum II.24–27) and was influential later on Cyril of Alexandria. His works survive primarily in Latin translation, with Greek fragments preserved in patristic quotations (TLG 1447).
record.label: Irenaeus of Lyon

record.description: The Carneadean echo is transposed into Christian terms in Adv. Haer. IV, 37, 1-2 (original text preserved by John of Damascus in the Hiera, ed. K. Holl, TU 20.2, p. 63): 'If some (as Valentin maintains) are evil by nature and others likewise good by nature, the latter should not be praised, even if they are good, since they were constituted such. Nor should the wicked be blamed, since they were made such.' For Amand, the argument is 'barely sketched' — Irenaeus mentions it 'for the sake of completeness' before developing the scriptural proof at length. The Christian transposition is clear: God replaces the Greek judges as the supreme regulator of morality, and the punishments are eternal (rather than temporal).

metadata.description_en: The Carneadean echo is transposed into Christian terms in Adv. Haer. IV, 37, 1-2 (original text preserved by John of Damascus in the Hiera, ed. K. Holl, TU 20.2, p. 63): 'If some (as Valentin maintains) are evil by nature and others likewise good by nature, the latter should not be praised, even if they are good, since they were constituted such. Nor should the wicked be blamed, since they were made such.' For Amand, the argument is 'barely sketched' — Irenaeus mentions it 'for the sake of completeness' before developing the scriptural proof at length. The Christian transposition is clear: God replaces the Greek judges as the supreme regulator of morality, and the punishments are eternal (rather than temporal).
metadata.description_en_pre_2026_08_16: Christianly transposed Carneadean echo in Adv. Haer. IV, 37, 1-2 (original text preserved by John of Damascus in the Hiera) : 'If some (as Valentinus claims) are evil by nature and others are equally good by nature, these should not be praised, even if they are good, for they were so constituted'. For Amand, the argument is 'barely sketched' — Irenaeus mentions it 'by conscience-clearing' before developing the scriptural proof at length
metadata.description_fr: Echo carneadien transpose chretiennement dans Adv. Haer. IV, 37, 1-2 (texte original conserve par Jean Damascene dans les Hiera, ed. K. Holl, TU 20.2, p. 63) : 'Si les uns (comme le pretend Valentin), sont mauvais par nature et si les autres sont bons egalement par nature, ceux-ci ne doivent point etre loues, meme s'ils sont bons, car ils ont ete constitues tels. Les mechants ne doivent pas non plus etre blames, puisqu'ils ont ete faits tels'. Pour Amand, l'argument est 'a peine esquisse' — Irenee le mentionne 'par acquit de conscience' avant de developper longuement la preuve scripturaire. La transposition chretienne est claire : Dieu remplace les juges grecs comme regulateur supreme de la moralite, et les sanctions sont eternelles (et non temporelles)

Holl, 'Fragmente vornicänischer Kirchenväter aus den Sacra Parallela', TU 20.2, 1899); D. Amand, 'Fatalisme et liberté dans l'antiquité grecque' (1945), pp. 222-223

record.description: Fürst 2022's thesis (Kap. IV 4-5, p. 178-186 ; Adv. Haer. IV 37,6-7 = FC 8/4, 328-330): Irenaeus of Lyons proclaims human free self-determination against the Gnostic conception of fixed "natures" (choïque/hylique/sarkique). The Irenaean argument takes the form of a reductio ad absurdum: if human beings were inevitably determined to possess a particular "nature" (natura) that would save or condemn them, "then good men have nothing particular about them, since they are such more by nature (natura) than by their own will (voluntas), and possess the good from themselves rather than through their own choice" (Adv. Haer. IV 37,6). According to Fürst, this anti-Gnostic polemic was the principal historical driving force behind the Christian Freiheitspathos: opposition to the Marcionites, Valentinians, Basilideans, and other schools advocating predestinarian doctrine led the apologists (Justin, Theophilus of Antioch, Tatian, Irenaeus, Clement, Tertullian) to elevate freedom to the status of a polemical issue of the first importance. Origen would inherit this polemical boundary (Princ. III 1,6 = the great refutation of Valentinian determinism).
record.label: Irénée défend la libre Selbstbestimmung contre les natures gnostiques fixes (Fürst 2022 Kap. IV 4-5)

metadata.description_fr: Thèse de Fürst 2022 (Kap. IV 4-5, p. 178-186 ; Adv. Haer. IV 37,6-7 = FC 8/4, 328-330) : Irénée de Lyon proclame la libre autodétermination de l'homme contre la conception gnostique des « natures » fixes (choïque/hylique/sarkique). L'argument irénéen est en forme de réduction à l'absurde : si les hommes étaient inévitablement déterminés à posséder une « nature » (natura) particulière qui les sauverait ou les perdrait, « alors les bons hommes ne représentent rien de particulier, parce qu'ils sont tels plus par nature (natura) que par leur propre volonté (voluntas) et possèdent le bien d'eux-mêmes plutôt que par leur propre choix » (Adv. Haer. IV 37,6). Cette polémique anti-gnostique est, selon Fürst, le principal moteur historique du Freiheitspathos chrétien : l'opposition aux Marcionites, Valentiniens, Basilidiens et autres écoles à doctrine prédestinationiste pousse les apologistes (Justin, Théophile d'Antioche, Tatien, Irénée, Clément, Tertullien) à élever la liberté au rang d'enjeu polémique de premier ordre. Origène héritera de cette frontière polémique (Princ. III 1,6 = la grande réfutation du déterminisme valentinien).
metadata.quote_de: Wenn Menschen unausweichlich darauf festgelegt wären, eine bestimmte „Natur“ (natura) zu haben … „dann stellen auch die guten Menschen nichts Besonderes dar, weil sie mehr von Natur aus (natura) als aus eigenem Willen (voluntas) so sind und das Gute von selbst haben und nicht auf eigene Wahl hin.“
metadata.quote_source_file: /Users/romaingirardi/Desktop/DOCTORAT/Doctorat SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/05_Origene/Alfons Fürst - Wege zur Freiheit_ Menschliche Selbstbestimmung von Homer bis Origenes-Mohr Siebeck (2022).md
metadata.quote_verbatim: Die Freiheit der Entscheidung, auf der die frühchristlichen Philosophen so entschieden bestanden, diente ihnen vor al­lem als Argument in ihrer Kritik am gnostischen Determi­nismus. In dieser Frontstellung dürfte der hauptsächliche Antrieb dafür zu sehen sein, weshalb die frühchristlichen Apologeten die Freiheit des Menschen derart eindringlich hervorhoben. Gegen die Festlegung des Menschen auf einen bestimmten Charakter, ein bestimmtes Schicksal, eine be­stimmte moralische oder religiöse Qualität, nämlich zu den Guten oder zu den Bösen, zu den Erlösten oder zu den Ver­dammten zu gehören, verteidigten sie auf der Linie des pla­tonischen Axioms, dass die Ursache für das persönliche Geschick nicht bei Gott, sondern beim Menschen zu suchen sei, die freie Bestimmung des Menschen über sich selbst, um so die Möglichkeit der Veränderung zu sichern und die Ver­antwortung für seine Taten und Untaten zu wahren. In diesem Sinne proklamierte Irenäus die freie Selbstbe­stimmung gegen die gnostische Vorstellung von festgeleg­ten „Naturen“ der einzelnen Menschen. Wenn Menschen, meinte er, unausweichlich darauf festgelegt wären, eine be­stimmte „Natur“ (natura) zu haben, zum Beispiel „irdisch“ (Choiker), „materiell“ (Hyliker) oder „fleischlich“ (Sarki­ker) zu sein, und deshalb am Ende der Welt aufgrund dieser „Natur“ vernichtet zu werden, „dann stellen auch die guten Menschen nichts Besonderes dar, weil sie mehr von Natur aus (natura) als aus eigenem Willen (voluntas) so sind und das Gute von selbst haben und nicht auf eigene Wahl hin.“
metadata.translation_en: If human beings were inevitably determined to possess a definite ‘nature’ (natura) … ‘then the good men represent nothing special, because they are such more by nature (natura) than by their own will (voluntas) and possess the good of themselves rather than by their own choice.’
metadata.verified_reference: Fürst 2022, Kap. IV 4-5 (Irenaeus material pp. 172-180); Irenaeus, Adv. haer. IV 37,6 (FC 8/4, 328) — the natura/voluntas quote — and IV 37,7 (FC 8/4, 330); also I 6,2 (FC 8/1,164) and IV 4,3 (FC 8/4, 36), all cited by Fürst.

record.description: Illud autem quod ait : Quotiens volui colligere filios tuos et noluisti, veterem legem libertatis hominis manifestavit, quia liberum eum Deus fecit, ab initio habentem suam potestatem sicut et suam animam, ad utendum sententia Dei voluntarie, et non coactum ab eo. Vis enim a Deo non fit, sed bona sententia adest illi semper. Et propter hoc consilium quidem bonum dat omnibus ; posuit autem in homine potestatem electionis, quemadmodum et in angelis - etenim angeli rationabiles -, uti hi quidem qui obaudissent juste bonum sint possidentes, datum quidem a Deo, servatum vero ab ipsis ; qui autem non obaudierunt juste non invenientur cum bono et meritam poenam percipient, quoniam Deus quidem dedit benigne bonum, ipsi vero non custodierunt diligenter illud neque pretiosum arbitrati sunt, sed supereminentiam bonitatis contempserunt. Abjicientes igitur bonum et quasi respuentes, merito omnes <in> justum judicium incident Dei, quemadmodum et Apostolus Paulus in ea epistola quae est ad Romanos testificatus est, dicens ita : An divitias bonitatis ejus et patientiae et longanimitatis contemnis, ignorans quoniam bonitas Dei in paenitentiam te adducit ? Secundum autem duritiam tuam et cor impaenitens thesaurizas tibimetipsi iram in die irae et revelationis justi judicii Dei. Gloria autem et honor, inquit, omni operanti bonum. Dedit ergo Deus bonum, quemadmodum et Apostolus testificatur in eadem epistola, et qui operantur quidem illud gloriam et honorem percipient, quoniam operati sunt bonum cum possint non operari illud, hi autem qui illud non operantur judicium justum excipient Dei, quoniam non sunt operati bonum cum possint operari illud.
record.label: Irenaeus, Adversus haereses IV.37.1 (ancient Latin; SC 100)

record.description: Propter hoc ergo signum salutis nostrae eum qui ex Virgine Emmanuel est, ipse <dedit> Dominus, quoniam ipse Dominus erat qui saluabat eos, quia per semetipsos non habebant saluari ; et propter hoc Paulus infirmitatem hominis adnuntians ait : Scio enim quoniam non inhabitat in carne mea bonum, significans quoniam non a nobis sed a Deo est bonum salutis nostrae ; et iterum : Miser ego homo, quis me liberabit de corpore mortis huius ? deinde infert Liberatorem ; Gratia Iesu Christi Domini nostri. Hoc autem et Esaias : Confortamini (inquit) manus resolutae et genua debilia, adhortamini, pusillanimes sensu, confortamini, ne timeatis ! Ecce, Deus noster iudicium retribuit et retributurus est. ipse ueniet et saluabit nos ; - hoc quoniam non a nobis sed a Dei adiumento habuimus saluari.

record.description: Si autem naturaliter quidam boni, quidam vero mali facti fuissent, neque hi laudabiles essent quia boni sunt, tales enim facti fuerant, sed neque illi vituperabiles, et ipsi enim tales fuerant instituti. Sed quoniam omnes ejusdem sunt naturae, et potentes retinere et operari bonum, et potentes rursum amittere id et non facere, juste etiam apud homines sensatos - quanto magis apud Deum - alii quidem laudantur et dignum percipiunt testimonium electionis bonae et perseverantiae, alii vero accusantur et dignum percipiunt damnum eo quod justum et bonum reprobaverint. Et ideo prophetae [bonum quoque] hortabantur homines justitiam agere bonumque operari, sicut per multa ostendimus, quia in nobis sit hoc et propter multam neglegentiam in oblivionem inciderimus et consilio egeamus bono ; propter quod bonus Deus praestabat bonum consilium per prophetas.

record.description: Εἰ φύσει οἱ μὲν φαῦλοι, οἱ δὲ ἀγαθοὶ γεγόνασιν, οὐθ' οὗτοι ἐπαινετοὶ ὄντες ἀγαθοί, τοιοῦτοι γὰρ κατεσκευάσθησαν, οὔτ' ἐκεῖνοι μεμπτοί, οὕτως γεγονότες. Ἀλλ' ἐπεὶ οἱ πάντες τῆς αὐτῆς εἰσι φύσεως, δυνάμενοί τε κατασχεῖν καὶ πρᾶξαι τὸ ἀγαθόν, καὶ δυνάμενοι πάλιν ἀποβαλεῖν αὐτὸ καὶ μὴ ποιῆσαι, δικαίως καὶ παρὰ ἀνθρώποις τοῖς εὐνομουμένοις, καὶ πολὺ πρότερον παρὰ θεῷ, οἱ μὲν ἐπαινοῦνται καὶ ἀξίας τυγχάνουσι μαρτυρίας τῆς τοῦ καλοῦ [καθόλου] ἐκλογῆς καὶ ἐπιμονῆς, οἱ δὲ καταιτιῶνται καὶ ἀξίως τυγχάνουσι ζημίας τῆς τοῦ καλοῦ καὶ ἀγαθοῦ ἀποβολῆς. Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο οἱ προφῆται παρῇνουν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις δικαιοπραγεῖν καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἐξεργάζεσθαι, ὡς ἐφ' ἡμῖν ὄντος τοῦ τοιούτου καὶ διὰ τὴν πολλὴν ἀμέλειαν εἰς λήθην ἐκπεπτωκότων καὶ γνώμης δεομένων ἀγαθῆς, ἣν ὁ ἀγαθὸς Θεὸς παρεῖχεν γνώμην διὰ τῶν προφητῶν. Ταῦτα γὰρ πάντα τὸ αὐτεξούσιον ἐπιδείκνυσι τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ τὸ συμβουλευτικὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀποτρέποντὸς μὲν τοῦ ἀπειθεῖν αὐτῷ, ἀλλὰ μὴ βιαζομένου.
